entries.title: Lords of Serendipity by Randy Boyagoda review – a campus satire for this moment of crisis
entries.summary: This propulsive, globe-trotting tale brilliantly skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parent
entries.content:
It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parents and professors, and their dealings with a common antagonist: the university.

The first character we meet is Sri Lankan teen Devi, who is set on obtaining offers from “Ochpys” – her acronym for Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale and Stanford. To help her realise her dream, Devi’s family of modest means – her mother, father, maternal grandmother and two brothers – hire themselves out as mourners at the funerals of the wealthy. Most of this money goes towards paying Johannes, her tutor on WhatsApp who, unbeknown to Devi, is a hard-up Indian student at Arcadia Tech, an undistinguished university in the US. Meanwhile, Jack, a statistician at the same institution, has taken on an additional teaching load to meet the fees of the elite college his daughter Katrina attends in New England. Soon he catches on to a grade-fixing scheme aimed at flailing international students, run by his teaching assistant Allard Hamburger. Jack is left in disbelief when, to buy his silence, the university puts him on paid administrative leave instead of launching an inquiry into a scandal that has left one student dead by suicide.

Boyagoda keeps the narrative charged with drama through an ever-evolving gallery of characters and their never-ending problems: yet-to-be-Dr Allard, who suffers from daddy issues and intends to endow a research chair at the Ivy League school where his long-absent father Martin teaches astronomy; his all-but-PhD mother Patricia, who had been teaching research methods to undergraduates until she was replaced by a chatbot named Puck; Katrina and her roommate Cham, a Sri Lankan refugee raised in Rome. The best of friends from the moment they met and shared their stories – Cham’s separation from her family and adoption by the Sri Lankan ambassador; Katrina’s mother laid low by breast cancer – the two are now quietly feuding. This is partly because they are unwelcome on university premises, thanks to Cham, whose idea it was that they sabotage a protest version of the 14th-century romance Sir Gawain and the Green Knight in a bid to be radical on their own terms. By sticking to the original script instead of observing a sit-in like the rest of the cast, they have partaken in a play that “perpetuates speciesist, sexist, racist, ableist, ageist and Christianist ideologies that are also deployed in support of settler-colonial Zionist apartheid fascist regimes”.

A campus novel of the present moment, Lords of Serendipity is animated by the upheavals reshaping American universities and the wider world: the pressures put on higher education by the Trump administration, the steady erosion of the humanities, Israel’s devastation of Gaza, as well as the threat of AI and the fact that “everything with substance and history, with texture and nuance, with seriousness, gravitas, was being replaced with flatness and shine and more flatness and shine”. Boyagoda has no end of things to say about “the corruption upon corruption upon corruption of the university”, its growing subordination to corporate interests, what is lost in that process, and how for many students from the global south a western education may not be “a lifestyle thing, or an experience” but an expensive pathway to immigration.

Part of what makes this book propulsive as well as engaging and thought-provoking beyond its topical significance is Boyagoda’s voice, which is intellectually agile without being self-congratulatory, and incisive without squandering its whimsy and impishness. Boyagoda, who is a professor of English at the University of Toronto, has both good and bad jokes, and he often wields them at his own expense, poking fun at everything from the interpretive excesses of English literature scholars to the proclivity of humanities folks to cast themselves as the “eternal torture victims of the university”.

Many things happen in this novel – too many to describe here. The most unexpected development concerns the Chinese takeover of a university in the Sri Lankan city of Kurunegala, which is renamed Serendipity in a grim and ironic evocation of the island’s colonial past (“Serendib,” we are told, “was the original name of Sri Lanka itself, when Europeans and Chinese explorers first found it and were so unexpectedly happy and amazed by their discovery”). The university becomes the new base for Martin’s work on colliding stars, after he abruptly loses his research chair at his home institution. Jack, who has been persuaded to join this new venture, will find himself once again at the centre of a scandal that puts his integrity to the test.

Meanwhile, after barely pulling through a series of dispiriting setbacks, Devi approaches Jack in the hope of turning her luck around. That we live in an unequal but interconnected world is hardly a revelation; in this tragicomic tale, full of crooks and strivers, opportunists, dreamers and mercurial patrons, Boyagoda’s genius lies in humanising this entanglement, and revealing its contradictions.

entries.title: ‘A trailblazer in the truest sense’: poet Grace Nichols wins £10,000 Pioneer prize
entries.summary: The Guyana-born, British-based writer takes home the Royal Society of Literature prize honouring women writers over 60 who have broken barriersThe poet Grace Nichols has been named the winner of the 2026 Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize, a £10,000 award that recognises women writers over 60 who broke through at a time when the literary world was less open to them.Nichols, 76, who was born
entries.content:
The poet Grace Nichols has been named the winner of the 2026 Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize, a £10,000 award that recognises women writers over 60 who broke through at a time when the literary world was less open to them.

Nichols, 76, who was born in Guyana and moved to the UK in 1977, made her name with I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, which took the Commonwealth poetry prize in 1983, and The Fat Black Woman’s Poems, a collection published the following year. Her poems have been GCSE set texts for decades, and she has written extensively for children as well as adults.

The Pioneer prize was established last year by the then president of the Royal Society of Literature (RSL), Bernardine Evaristo, who donated the £100,000 she received from the 2025 Women’s prize outstanding contribution award to fund it for 10 years. The award will rotate between forms each year, and this year was given for poetry. The winner of the inaugural Pioneer prize was the novelist, playwright and activist Maureen Duffy, who died in May.

Nichols’ poems draw on Guyanese folk tales, oral tradition, landscape, and on the history of slavery. She was also one of a group of West Indian poets whose work tackled racial tensions during a time of inflammatory immigration debates in Thatcher’s Britain. Her other collections include Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (1989), Sunris (1996), which won the Guyana poetry prize, and Startling the Flying Fish (2005). She has also published a novel, Whole of a Morning Sky (1986), as well as books for younger readers including Come on Into My Tropical Garden (1988) and Give Yourself a Hug (1994). Several of those were anthologies she co-edited with her partner, fellow Guyanese poet John Agard.

Ruth Borthwick, the chair of English PEN, who led the judging panel, called Nichols “one of our most important contemporary poets”, who had developed “her own poetic language – an earthy mix of Creole and standard English”.

“Grace showed the way for generations of poets from the diaspora to make the cultural connections between the Caribbean and Britain,” Borthwick said.

Borthwick was joined on the panel by the poet Sarah Howe, who said: “Grace Nichols is a legend, a trailblazer in the truest sense. Her work spans continents and traditions, alive to orality and shapely on the page, light and weighty at once. Her work blends the rhythms and stories of her Caribbean heritage with a unique vision of modern Britain.”

Nichols said she had been surprised to get the call from Borthwick. “I am honoured and delighted to have the RSL Pioneer prize bestowed on me and grateful to poetry for all that it’s given me, as well as to the judges and my parents who made books a part of our lives,” she said.

Judith Palmer, the director of the Poetry Society, also on the judging panel, said Nichols “was probably the first poet who really lifted poetry off the page for me”.

When she established the prize, Evaristo said: “It’s very easy to forget the feminist struggles of the past and the intrepid women who paved the way for successive generations, and it’s important to celebrate our trailblazers while they are still around to enjoy it.”

Nichols, who is a vice-president of the RSL, received the Queen’s gold medal for poetry in 2021. Her next collection for adults, The Tracks of My Name, will be published on 19 November.

She will be celebrated at an event at the British Library on 1 March 2027.

entries.title: Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter review – Kardashian under the microscope
entries.summary: The author gets a backstage pass to the personal life of the world’s most famous woman – but what do we really learn?The magazine writer Jonathan Van Meter profiles very famous people for extremely glossy publications. He was responsible for the notorious 1990 interview in which supermodel Linda Evangelista said she wouldn’t wake up for less than $10,000 a day, and in recent years, he has intervie
entries.content:
The magazine writer Jonathan Van Meter profiles very famous people for extremely glossy publications. He was responsible for the notorious 1990 interview in which supermodel Linda Evangelista said she wouldn’t wake up for less than $10,000 a day, and in recent years, he has interviewed Taylor Swift, Michelle Obama and Lady Gaga for American Vogue. In 2019, he wrote a cover story, also for Vogue, on Kim Kardashian, the reality TV star turned business­woman turned criminal justice activist, and one of the most famous women in the world. In the lengthy acknowledgments to this book, he describes receiving a phonecall from her after the piece had been published. “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you,” she told him. He replied by telling her that he was going to write a book about her, “whether you like it or not!”

Spoiler alert: she liked it. And the concept underlying the book can be justified: Kim Kardashian really has transformed celebrity culture. Her family, broadcasting their lives for years, came to define contemporary reality television, beginning with Keeping Up With the Kardashians in 2007 and continuing to the present day with The Kardashians. She saw the potential in social media and used it to her advantage from its inception. Last year, her clothing line, Skims, was valued at $5bn (£3.75bn). Van Meter notes that despite her ubiquitous presence, there has been “a dearth of well-written profiles and shrewd cultural analysis” about the phenomenon of Kim K.

But what is promised and what is delivered are not exactly the same. Early on, Van Meter references Kant and the academic Timothy Morton, and later, he invokes Joan Didion’s writing on Hollywood. But any attempts at cultural analysis, shrewd or otherwise, quickly fall away in favour of a more traditional in-depth biography, its wheels greased by regular, intimate access to the Kardashians and many of Kim’s closest friends and colleagues.

Van Meter visits his subject often, at her many homes and places of work. They talk over snacks and coffee. Kim may be in her pyjamas or a bathrobe, having just got out of the shower. At one point, she does away with the formality of clothing entirely. “I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched,” he writes, describing a day spent with her at a photoshoot. This is intended to suggest candour, though inevitably it implies a lack of critical distance. At the end, in the acknowledgements, he thanks her for her “time, but more so, your trust”.

Van Meter notes that Kim does not like to dwell on the bad stuff, nor does she seem particularly inclined towards introspection. What more is there to say about her life that has not already been televised? Ironically, her views on the family’s show may be the most fascinating part of this book. Doing television has been good for them, she says, “because we’re not going to leave an episode unfinished” – by which she means that arguments are almost always resolved, because they have to be, for the shape of the TV narrative. Public and private are one and the same.

At its best, the book does expose some of the Kardashian family’s gothic underbelly. In 1995, Kim’s mother and father found themselves on opposing sides of the OJ Simpson murder trial (Kris Jenner supported her best friend Nicole Brown’s family during the trial, while her ex-husband, the late Robert Kardashian, was on Simpson’s legal team). For a while, Kim’s teenage boyfriend was TJ Jackson, nephew of Michael, whose own family lore is horrifying and unique. Her school days are likened to the movie Clueless, but there is a touch of Bret Easton Ellis in there, too.

There is some reflection on the sex tape that propelled Kim into the public eye (it has left her with “a lot to prove”, she says). Van Meter offers a pop-psychology analysis of why she seems to gravitate towards “lost boys”, and she talks about her marriage to Kanye West, albeit with respect and restraint. She describes a move away from a more materialistic worldview after being robbed at gunpoint in Paris, in 2016. The book ends with speculation that she might run for political office. “I am so flattered,” she responds, and leaves the prospect open.

There are moments of camp extravagance. One chapter begins, “Did the trouble start with not one, but two boob jobs?” Van Meter namedrops Anna Wintour, Oprah Winfrey and his own tennis coach. But elsewhere, the narrative swoons and fawns. Kim’s private jet is “a shade of nudey grey,” we learn. “Which is so me,” she says. It is also so this book. The Kardashian aura must be strong, because reading this evokes the same sensation as watching their show: it is seductive, hypnotic, but possessed of a sleight of hand that turns everything beige.

entries.title: Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg review – a BBC reporter’s howl of frustration
entries.summary: After more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politicsLaura Kuenssberg always swore she would never write a book. Amid all the vitriol hurled her way, the BBC’s political editor turned presenter has largely kept her counsel. She rarely complained even when she needed security to do her job unobstructed at Labour party conference under Jere
entries.content:
Laura Kuenssberg always swore she would never write a book. Amid all the vitriol hurled her way, the BBC’s political editor turned presenter has largely kept her counsel. She rarely complained even when she needed security to do her job unobstructed at Labour party conference under Jeremy Corbyn, or had to run the gauntlet of aggressive Brexit protesters outside parliament, or when a creepy unnamed minister tried to inveigle her into his hotel room for what an appalled Kuenssberg concluded was intended to be a threesome. Knowing everything she does is minutely parsed for bias, she keeps her cards close to her chest. Until, apparently, something snapped.

Pay Attention is a muted but heartfelt howl of frustration with politicians “who have looked like an absolute shower for a long time” but also, sotto voce, with voters, who she evidently wishes would occasionally take things more seriously. Having covered Westminster since the late noughties, Kuenssberg brings all that weight of experience to bear in spelling out just how far the abnormal is now becoming normalised in British politics.

Once, she points out, there was a cross-party understanding not to inflame racial tensions at sensitive times; now masked men can roam Belfast seeking foreign-born people to burn from their homes, and still Nigel Farage says they shouldn’t be called far right. The Greens, Tories and Reform all selected candidates for this year’s council elections who had previously expressed startlingly flaky views. The rapid turnover of prime ministers over the last decade isn’t normal either, she argues, but nor was the behaviour causing it – from the boozy loucheness of Boris Johnson’s Downing Street to Keir Starmer securing a whopping great majority but no mandate, having never really made a case for what he actually wanted to do.

This is a serious and earnest book, not a gossipy insider’s tale, focused on the failures of governance that have radicalised what she argues isn’t naturally a radical country. Kuenssberg describes a politics paralysed by fear, with MPs afraid of telling an angry public the hard truths they’ll happily discuss with her once the camera stops running. (Nobody she talks to, apparently, thinks government operates effectively or spends money well.) But there are glimpses too of journalism struggling to hold politicians accountable, in an era of shrinking audience attention spans – Kuenssberg is notably sniffy about fluffy interviews that focus on a politician’s colourful backstory, not their policies – and Trumpian resistance to scrutiny.

She deconstructs the techniques Farage has developed to dodge questions he dislikes: expressing total conviction even when he doesn’t know the facts; turning questions back on his interviewer; and claiming to be persecuted by the media when cornered – an incendiary tactic Corbyn also adopted and which Zack Polanski is beginning to use, though Kuenssberg says at least Polanski has a “swagger and a bluntness” which means he’ll usually answer a straight question. When a politician lashes out at the mainstream media, she argues, pay extra attention to what they’re actually doing: often it’s a distraction tactic.

But she also identifies the weaknesses in mainstream politics that she believes gave Farage his opening. Ten years ago, she argues, it would have sounded “distressing and insane” to say there would soon be mass small boat crossings of the Channel: if that reality has changed, alongside the numbers of legal immigrants arriving and arrangements for housing them, perhaps it’s unsurprising that the public mood has changed, too. For Kuenssberg, it started with a wave of eastern European migration in the 2000s that some communities struggled to absorb, followed by the 2015 exodus of refugees from war-torn Syria and European leaders’ apparent impotence in the face of what she calls a “massive migration crisis”.

Politicians reacted first too slowly then too bombastically, promising to stop the boats and smash the gangs even when that wasn’t realistically possible, and fuelling the idea that immigration was beyond their control. What’s interesting about this argument – with which readers may agree or disagree – is that it is an argument, one of the few times she seemingly feels strongly enough to advance one.

There is a discernible tension here between Kuenssberg’s professional duty as a BBC journalist to remain politically neutral, and the need for a book to say something beyond the bleeding obvious. At times, I wondered if she wouldn’t have been better saving it all for a post-BBC memoir where she could let rip.

As it is, some readers will be outraged that she isn’t taking a stronger stand against extremism, while others will doubtless think she has outed herself as a moderate centrist merely by pointing out that ideas now advanced by both Reform and the Greens would once have been considered completely off the wall. As Kuenssberg knows better than most, you can’t win – though that doesn’t mean it isn’t worth trying. Sadly, I think she’s right that our politics is neither normal nor healthy, and that saying so in plain English is an important part of holding the line. But it will take more than paying attention, I suspect, to bring sanity back.

entries.title: The Rhyl Poster by Tom McCarthy review – is this avant-garde spy drama worth the riddles?
entries.summary: The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating readingOf the cohort of experimental novelists whose renown grew in the wake of the 2008 financial crash – names include Deborah Levy, Eimear McBride and Claire-Louise Bennett – it was Tom McCarthy who first demonstrated the benefit of bypassing orthodox routes to market. When British publishers rej
entries.content:
Of the cohort of experimental novelists whose renown grew in the wake of the 2008 financial crash – names include Deborah Levy, Eimear McBride and Claire-Louise Bennett – it was Tom McCarthy who first demonstrated the benefit of bypassing orthodox routes to market. When British publishers rejected his 2005 novel, Remainder, about an amnesiac who spends a windfall restaging his past, he released it in a limited edition from a Paris art collective. Three years later, Zadie Smith wrote an essay celebrating it as a path-breaking overthrow of establishment-sanctioned “lyrical realism”. The literary press soon began finding more room for McCarthy, whose regular denunciations of English fiction – not least for its “middlebrow” ignorance of challenging ideas from the continent – did much to shape bookish conversation at the turn of the decade.

If his zeal wasn’t to everyone’s taste – the New Statesman once called him Britain’s “most galling interviewee” – anyone lately stepping into a bookshop might well feel the last laugh belongs to McCarthy. Witness the success of Fitzcarraldo Editions: innovative Europeans are hot property. Risk-rewarding ventures such as the Goldsmiths prize, established in 2013 to spotlight formally daring fiction amid panic about the philistinism of award panels, feel a little less urgent when a novel as inscrutable as M John Harrison’s The End of Everything sits comfortably on this year’s Booker shortlist, a bestseller to boot. When the mainstream and the avant garde are now kissing cousins, where does it leave McCarthy? The Making of Incarnation (2021), a dense, Pynchonesque espionage yarn about motion capture technology, suggested that he saw the Booker-shortlisted success of both 2010’s C and 2015’s Satin Island as a green light to push readers harder. Further evidence for the theory is supplied by his riddling new novel, The Rhyl Poster, another abstruse spy drama, this time set deep inside the polyglot operations of Luxembourg’s Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). It’s as if McCarthy – a longtime Berliner who, post-Brexit, holds a Swedish passport – had determined to immerse himself in the minutiae of the institution his native Britain elected to leave.

We’re in the company of a pill-popping jurist, Stanton, scarred by his past as a military geographer with the British army in Iraq. Memories of that time, opaque to the reader, don’t help him at work, where he’s meant to be drafting a landmark opinion on a privacy suit against a data analytics firm. His desire for relief from his various war wounds makes him prey to an approach from a shadowy criminal seeking EU documents in exchange for unapproved painkillers from a lab in Rotterdam – home, handily, to Stanton’s long-distance Dutch-Surinamese girlfriend, one among a catalogue of lovers whose pillow talk greases the story’s cogs.

The ensuing double-dealing zigzag around northern Europe plays out as a genre-curious mashup of trauma plot and heist narrative, steadfastly averse to closure. Suspense derives less from events than from the disorientingly stretchy syntax of McCarthy’s narration, a dry blend of legal lingo and lower-slung idiom, like a lecturer wearing a blazer with Nikes. “Interpretation,” we’re told, isn’t the same thing as “advancing to a conclusion from a set of givens guided by parameters that, fixed, are also given: that’s induction. No: interpretation, understood in its profoundest sense, is the plumb opposite … If law in general is the realm where language shapes the world, the European Court of Justice pimps this logic to the nth.”

The novel’s interest in law, or its “fundamental propensity for repeatability, its driving imperative towards self-duplication”, eventually reveals itself as another iteration of McCarthy’s abiding preoccupation with repetition. Even the most dramatic scene, a revelatory flashback to Stanton’s days in Iraq, is a replay of sorts, evoking Zadie Smith’s observation about the role Remainder gave to a black man’s fatal shooting (experimental or not, she said, “the non-white subject is still the bad conscience of the contemporary novel”).

Remainder remains McCarthy’s best book, its multifunctional concept delivering old-school psychological intrigue while poking fun at literary realism’s mimetic aspirations. Reading The Rhyl Poster, by contrast, is like trying to fill in a crossword using the wrong clues. The endeavour isn’t devoid of quixotic frisson: it’s not unfun to note, for instance, that the defendant in Stanton’s case is named Elrond – like Palantir, a lift from Tolkien – or that the claimant, Kohlhas, described as a “one-man operation”, echoes the wronged justice-seeker Michael Kohlhaas in Heinrich von Kleist’s 1810 novella of that name.

Yet these are keys tinkling, not doors unlocked, and while there’s a measure of page-turning urgency in Stanton’s increasingly hallucinatory personal crisis, he’s too plainly a parody of a girl-getting hardman-savant to carry much by way of emotional weight. The mystifying title, poised between enigma and bathos, refers (no spoiler, this) to the protagonist’s half-memory of riding a train in north Wales while watching someone paste up an advert – blank, naturally.

The prank-adjacent vibe hardly subsides once the novel’s 240 pages of high-pressure buildup conclude with the word “begin”. Any takeaway perhaps lies in the acronym of the court at the book’s heart, blinking like a beacon through its pages – CJEU, c’est jeu, a game – and if you don’t get a kick out of that, be sure McCarthy does.

entries.title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag
entries.summary: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourselfRecently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space trav
entries.content:
Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round!”

It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones.

How did things get so bad? I believe the answer is, in part, that we’re constantly exposed to a novel form of charisma. As a psychiatrist, I’ve always been fascinated by this quality: the magnetism that brings out a deep sense of trust, loyalty or enthusiasm in others. The psychology of charisma tells us that it is not necessarily a magic, undefinable X-factor, but rather a set of skills and behaviours. Sometimes people have it naturally, sometimes people learn it.

I have some experience with this. When I started my podcast a few years ago, I struggled (as I still do) with my monotonous voice. All the content creation experts said the same thing: switch up the pitch, pace and volume of your speech to maximise audience engagement. Slick production is optional, charismatic communication is not. Storytelling, body language, moral outrage and more can be mastered to help would-be internet personalities put a spell on their audience.

It’s been a huge lesson for me to discover how difficult it can be to discuss big topics in the mental health space responsibly, even as a trained professional. It’s also become shockingly clear how easily someone can distort the truth on, say, antidepressants, psychotherapy or ADHD when they have no experience or knowledge in that area – as long as they come across confidently and convincingly.

The dangers of charisma are nothing new, of course. History is filled with examples of people using charm to advance their interests. Dictators, cult leaders and con artists are all proof that an otherwise reasonable person can succumb to a well-executed charm offensive.

The difference now is one of scale. The 2024 US election, for example, was widely described as the “podcast election”, as both candidates (Trump more successfully) consented to numerous softball interviews on the medium. They reached millions, not with policy, but with good vibes. And you don’t have to be a public figure to leverage charm in this way – any video with the right allure can go viral, regardless of that person’s intentions or expertise.

Why are we so easily taken in by charisma? Like many aspects of our psychology, we can understand it more clearly through the lens of our evolutionary past.

Our ancestors spent most of their time (approximately 94% of human history) as hunter-gatherers, living in nomadic tribes that may have consisted of as few as 20 people. Groups that small, pitted against the forces of nature, needed strong leadership. Like many animals, humans have status hierarchies. High-status hunter-gatherers likely had many of the traits we still associate with charisma today: great eye contact, body language that signalled certainty, a persuasive voice.

The difference being that, back then, you had the opportunity to observe your peers all day, every day: their flaws, their virtues, their competence, often while facing lethal danger. If a person was merely superficially charming, you found out quickly. Charisma would only win out if accompanied by other important qualities, including sound judgment, good character and wisdom.

That’s not the case now. Technology allows us to shield the unpalatable parts of ourselves much more easily, selecting only the best bits for public consumption. Our brains did not evolve to process handpicked slices of someone else’s behaviour, detached from the rest of their lives, so we’re vulnerable to being duped. One frightening example is that of Ruby Franke, the parenting vlogger with millions of subscribers who was jailed for child abuse after two of her six children were found beaten and malnourished.

We spend a lot of time worrying about how the minds of teenagers are warped by the online world. We’re keenly aware how prone they are to manipulation by seemingly impressive figures. What we fail to realise is, we’re all teenagers when it comes to the internet. Algorithmic social media has only been around for about 15 years, and we remain largely unconscious of how routinely it bypasses our better judgment. Is there any way to grow out of this newly acquired susceptibility?

The best form of defence against the excesses of charisma is critical thinking. We should regard it as being like a collective immune system, and it should be central to our culture and the way we educate our young people. They should be taught how to evaluate sources, interpret information and recognise bias. Similarly, separating confidence from substance ought to be considered a basic life skill. Looking at counter-arguments when we are emotionally pulled to someone’s perspective should be routine, and changing our mind when it is emotionally difficult should be celebrated.

It would also be helpful for the average person to learn the fundamentals of confident communication. Not only can this help you express yourself when you have something of real value to offer, but it also teaches you to see through a person who would happily use such tactics to deceive or seduce.

All told, charisma should actually be a red flag that encourages us to be more sceptical of an individual, not less. When someone can convincingly hold court on important topics like finance, healthcare or the Middle East, we should ask questions. What experience do they have? Do they have a history of dishonesty? What do they stand to gain from this view? What need in me might this person be speaking to? For my part, the next time I discuss something important, I will go easy on the pitch, pace and volume, and try to let the facts speak for themselves.

Alex Curmi is a psychiatrist and host of The Thinking Mind podcast.

Further reading

Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman (Penguin, £16.99)

The Age of Magical Overthinking by Amanda Montell (Thorsons, £12.99)

The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt (Penguin, £12.99)

entries.title: Like many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote back
entries.summary: The novelist receives passionate AI-written emails almost every day – but when he decided to take up one sender’s offer to find him new readers, the story took a darker turnThere’s no humble way to say it: I get a lot of fan mail. Almost every day, multi-paragraph emails arrive from passionate and well-informed readers in Barcelona and Frankfurt, Chicago and Warsaw. They have appealing names like
entries.content:
There’s no humble way to say it: I get a lot of fan mail. Almost every day, multi-paragraph emails arrive from passionate and well-informed readers in Barcelona and Frankfurt, Chicago and Warsaw. They have appealing names like Bella Monroe, Thalina Rose and Tricia Claxton. Some of them are straightforward enthusiasts while others are more irreverent, like the one who signs off her messages “warm chaos”. Some love the “deadpan genius” of my novels while others admire my nonfiction’s “moral courage”. What they all have in common, though, is that they are entirely fake and trying to con me out of money. They promise to promote my work at their city-wide book clubs or spread the word among their reading communities, if only I transfer a few hundred dollars to cover costs.

In the age of generative AI, scam emails have achieved a new level of personalisation. Most writers I know are receiving a steady stream of emails like this. The messages are often sophisticated enough to bypass a spam filter and reach our inboxes, leaving us no option but to read them and ask the painful question: would any real, living person feel this strongly about my work? Or, as one writer friend put it, the reason I know they’re fake is because they’ve actually read all my books.

What makes it worse is that the AIs that help write these scams really have read all our books. Last year, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn in compensation to the thousands of authors whose copyrighted work they’d used to train their AI, Claude. In July, a group of publishers filed a lawsuit against Google for utilising “one of the most prolific infringements of copyrighted materials in history” in order to train their AI, Gemini. So when writers receive these AI-assisted scam messages, we know we are being manipulated by a version of ourselves.

A few months ago, for example, I received a gushing email from Ottessa Moshfegh. The bestselling, Booker-shortlisted author of My Year of Rest and Relaxation – to my mind one of the most potent voices in contemporary fiction – was taking time away from producing her inimitable prose to write me a fan letter. I thanked her for getting in touch. We got chatting and I asked about her work-in-progress. She said that her new novel was “preoccupied with interior life: how emotions register, how they fail to, and what that absence or excess does to identity over time”. I thought we were making a real connection when she said that, really, the best way to understand her work was to explore her Amazon page. Sigh. Never meet your heroes. Other writers have received similar messages from fake Donna Tartt and fake Sally Rooney. It must be strange for the real Moshfegh, Rooney and Tartt to know that their novels have been harvested by tech corporations in order to create the ghost versions of themselves who now haunt the inboxes of their peers.

The correct response to all this is, of course, to simply report the email, block the sender and move on. But there is a part of me that fantasises about dramatically unmasking the scammer, revealing the villain beneath. So when I received an email from the founder of the Berlin Book Club, I decided to see how far I could get. I agreed that I did need help reaching new audiences. I was willing to pay for her connections and expertise. Soon we started discussing payment methods. She wanted me to use CashApp or make a direct bank transfer but I was insistent that I could only send hard cash. We went back and forth for a couple of days. I impressed on her that I had, at that very moment, 500 US dollars in crisp notes in an unmarked envelope and that I lived quite near the post office. She finally relented and gave me a physical address. Neither of us commented on how unusual it was for the founder of the Berlin Book Club to have a postal address in the Philippines. I went on Google Maps and was able to find the street in question, a rural two-lane road with palm trees, a junk shop, an evangelical church and a large building hidden behind high white walls.

The Philippines – along with Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia – is one of the countries most affected by organised crime networks running industrial-scale “scam farms”. Last year, authorities raided a facility in Bamban, north of Manila, freeing nearly 700 people who had been trapped there and forced to work as scammers. Inside the building, it resembled a hybrid between a call centre and a prison, rows upon rows of computers and green screens, and tiny dorms with bunk beds. About half of the workers were Filipino, while the others had been trafficked from China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Taiwan, Indonesia and Rwanda, their documentation withheld. The bosses, meanwhile, splashed around in the swimming pool next door. When another nearby compound was raided, they found it had its own brothel, karaoke suite and torture room. Across south-east Asia, these scam compounds are a multi-billion dollar industry, run largely by Chinese crime syndicates who routinely use violence and sexual abuse to keep workers in line. With the enormous sums of stolen money flowing through the industry, some compounds are the size of small towns or, perhaps more accurately, labour camps – with thousands of workers.

The scammers are encouraged to make use of the latest technology, not just generative AI but also face masking apps, so that they can conduct video calls wearing whatever face suits the task. The big focus is on “pig butchering”: long-term romance scams where people are tricked into falling in love with a wealthy, glamorous foreigner who then advises them to invest in fake cryptocurrency. When a large scam compound in Cambodia was seized by the Thai army, they discovered that its facilities resembled a TV studio. There were costumes, wigs and different sets for filming different scams. There was a fake Brazilian police station and a replica Vietnamese bank. Scammers were trained to keep their targets on the hook for months, even years, inventing private and personalised narrative worlds through which they could drain all of the victim’s money. In an interview with the BBC, one former scam compound manager sounded not unlike a novelist when he described the process. “[It’s] all about exploiting emotion,” he said. “You create a dream.”

For my part, I did not send any cash to the Philippines. Instead I shared the details I’d received with the country’s cybercrime agency. Although, in the words of Winston Casio, the spokesman for the presidential anti-organised crime commission in the Philippines, the ongoing problem is that the criminals have “the financial capability to corrupt just about anybody in public office. The amount of money they have is their potent tool against law enforcement.” When authorities shut down the Bamban compound, for example, they discovered that it was being run by Alice Guo, the local mayor. Similarly, the idea that AI companies might go out of their way to halt the criminal misuse of their technology seems just as doubtful – and for exactly the same reason. It’s making them fantastically rich.

All of which is to say that my fantasy of unmasking the villain was just that, a fantasy. At least now, when I receive fake fan mail, I can attempt to understand the probable reality behind the quirky name and upbeat tone. On the other side of the screen, there is someone frightened and far from home, sitting in a sound-insulated booth with a dozen phones splayed out on their desk – while behind them their manager walks by, a taser at his hip.

entries.title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October
entries.summary: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. entries.content:
Ian Rankin, author

I’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’s Like a Cat Loves a Bird was a winning blend of detail and readability.

A Bad, Bad Place by Frances Crawford is a prize-winning debut crime novel set in 1970s Glasgow. It’s clever, authentic and humane with unforgettable protagonists and pitch-black humour.

The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

David, Guardian reader

I’ve loved (most of) China Miéville’s books (I think that he and Alan Moore are the real doyens of “weird” fiction) – but The Rouse is surely his opus: sometimes prose-poetry, sometimes stream-of-consciousness, with shades (literally) of Lovecraft and MR James running through a bleak, unsettling yet compelling tale. I strongly suggest you take a very deep breath and launch into an adventure (lasting more than 1,200 pages) that will leave you dazed and amazed!

Louise Kennedy, author

I normally read one book at a time but, perhaps because I am on the road at the moment, I have three on the go. Emma Cline’s short story Arcadia almost killed me, and I’ve been a devotee ever since. Switzy, her new novel, accompanies on his final journey a man whose wealth and privilege offer no protection from the dementia that has begun to addle his poor brain. Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth: so far, charming, pretty Lily Bart is in charge of her story, but an encounter with a man who appears not to wish her well suggests there may be trouble ahead. John McGahern’s Memoir already has my heart rent in twain, to paraphrase an old Irish ballad, and he hasn’t even finished primary school.

Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Sophie, Guardian reader

Almost Life by Kiran Millwood Hargrave is a beautiful and heartbreaking love story that transported me back in time to Paris in the late 1970s and 80s. The main characters, Laure and Erica, as well as the other characters, soon feel like friends – friends who are human and imperfect, and who sometimes make frustrating decisions, but who are all the more lovable for it. It’s elegantly and smartly written, and paints such vivid pictures – I rarely read past my bedtime these days, but I stayed up late for this one, torn between wanting to finish and never wanting the book to end. It captures the feeling of love and being in love so well.

Mark, Guardian reader

This year, I’ve set myself the challenge of only reading books by writers who aren’t part of the Anglosphere, with each writer being from a different country. It’s certainly forced me to read stuff outside my comfort zone – which is how, this month, I’ve ended up reading Independent People by Halldór Laxness, a 500+ page novel about an Icelandic farming family. Over the course of about 20 years in the early 20th century, we follow the hardships and privations of a stubborn farmer who insists he fend for himself to maintain independence on his own land.

I expected this book to be unrelentingly grim reading – and in parts it is, especially in the almost indifference to death. But it’s also very humorous in its characters’ cynicism towards one another. It’s beautifully atmospheric in its prose, particularly the changing of the seasons and their effect on the dramatic landscape of the farm. Reading so much literature in translation has given me an appreciation of when it’s done well (without ever knowing the original text), and the translation by JA Thompson, in collaboration with Laxness, is sublime.
